title: TB8-17259
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX(Principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX(Associate Appellant(s)), citizens of Pakistan, appealed a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated March 19, 2018, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative of the principal Appellant was adopted by all of the Appellants. They alleged in the BOC that the principal Appellant owned a XXXX XXXX in Karachi, and that beginning in XXXX 2011 he was subjected to extortion demands from XXXX XXXX, an organized crime group affiliated with the political party XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. They alleged that in XXXX 2013 members of XXXX XXXX began to demand monthly payments and the principal Appellant was forced to agree to pay ?XXXX XXXX XXXX monthly.

The son of the principal Appellant (the associate Appellant) was kidnapped in XXXX 2014 and released upon payment of XXXX lakhs in a ransom. In XXXX 2015 the principal Appellant was required to pay XXXX XXXX XXXX and was granted XXXX days to acquire this money. Before the end of that period he closed his XXXX and the family moved to Lahore for safety in XXXX 2015.

While in Lahore, the principal Appellant was required to pay bribes to the police on two occasions. The Appellants returned to Karachi in XXXX 2015 and resided with the principal Appellant's in-laws. The family did not resume school or employment and decided to leave the country. The whole family eventually arrived in Canada and made a refugee claim.

The Appellants have been advised by their neighbours in Karachi that strangers have asked about the principal Appellant two or three times. They alleged that their nephew was accosted by men looking for the principal Appellant, when he went to check on their home.

The claim for refugee protection was heard by the RPD on February 28, 2018. In a written decision dated March 19, 2018 the RPD rejected the claim finding that the Appellants have a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Islamabad.
The Appellants argue that they were misrepresented by their former counsel and have filed a formal complaint against her with the Law Society of Alberta.

The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in failing to apply the Chairperson's Guidelines on Child Refugee Claimants1 and by not determining the impact of the Convention on the Rights of the Child on the minor Appellants' claims; the RPD's assessment of their personal evidence was unreasonable, incorrect and in breach of procedural fairness; that there was a breach of natural justice due to the incompetence of their former counsel; and that the RPD failed to assess and consider the evidence and provide a forward-looking assessment of risk. ADMISSIBILITY OF NEW EVIDENCE PRESENTED ON APPEAL

As provided for in subsection 110(3) of the IRPA, with certain exceptions, the RAD must proceed without a hearing on the basis of the record of the proceedings of the RPD, and may accept documentary evidence and written submissions from the Minister and the person who is the subject of the appeal. Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim, or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

The Appellants request that letters from a friend, XXXX XXXX XXXX, the principal Appellant's sister-in-law, and a letter from another friend, XXXX XXXX, be entered into evidence.2 The RAD will accept these letters as they postdate the rejection of the claim and address the issues relevant to the claim. The RAD will assess the weight to be assigned to these letters in its analysis of the appeal.

The Appellants request that a letter 3from a lawyer based in Karachi be entered into evidence. The RAD will accept this letter as it postdates the rejection of the claim and deals with relevant issues. The RAD will assess the weight to be put to this letter in its analysis of the appeal.

Attached to the letter from the lawyer are newspaper articles and a recent First Information Report (FIR). The RAD will only accept some of these items into evidence. These items are the article from the Weekly JANG dated XXXX XXXX, 2018; the article from the National dated XXXX XXXX, 2018; and the article from Dawn, dated XXXX XXXX, 2018. All of the other news items submitted predate the rejection of the claim and deal with issues that were already before the RPD. It is reasonable to expect in these circumstances that these items would have been submitted prior to the rejection of the claim. The RAD will not accept the FIR4 into evidence as it predates the rejection of the claim and would reasonably have been available through the same source that provided it in June 2018. Two of the newspaper articles do not reveal the name of the publication and so will not be accepted into evidence as it is not possible to assess the probative value of the items without knowing where they appeared.5

The Appellants have additionally provided photographs of the principal Appellant attending a demonstration in Canada against Pakistan in 2017. They have provided a newspaper article from 2017 referring to this protest.6 The RAD will not accept these documents into evidence given that they predate the rejection of the claim and would have been reasonably available to the Appellants at the time of their hearing.

The Appellants ask that a Response to Information Request from 20127 dealing with the situation and treatment of Mohajirs be entered into evidence. The RAD will accept this document given that it is an IRB document which has appeared in previous versions of the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Pakistan. Rule 29 of the RAD Rules

Rule 29 allows the Appellant to make an Application to provide a document not previously provided. Such an application must include an explanation of how the document meets the requirements of section 110(4) of the IRPA and how that evidence relates to the Appellant.8 In determining the Application, the RAD must consider any relevant factors, including the relevance and probative value of the document, any new evidence the document brings to the appeal, and whether the Appellant could have, with reasonable effort, provided the document with the Appellant's Record.

The Appellants ask that a letter from the principal Appellant's wife (the associate Appellant); a letter from her sister; and twelve newspaper articles be entered into evidence. In her affidavit, the associate Appellant stated that since the filing of the RAD appeal, the Appellants have researched and found new evidence regarding country conditions in Pakistan. The RAD will accept these items into evidence as they postdate the submission of the appeal and are relevant to country conditions in Pakistan. Oral Hearing

The RAD has considered whether an oral hearing should be held based on this new evidence. The RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in section 110(3) that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal, is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim, and, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.9
The RAD is able to consider the new evidence and assess its probative value without holding an oral hearing. Therefore, the RAD chooses not to hold a hearing under 110(6). ANALYSIS Former Counsel

The Appellants have made several allegations regarding their former counsel's conduct and competence during their RPD process. They have provided a copy of the complaint they made to the Law Society of Alberta about their former counsel, XXXX XXXX. This complaint contains fifteen points relating to how the Appellants believe their counsel failed them. These points are reflected in the Memorandum of Appeal. The Appellants submit that there was a breach of natural justice due to the incompetence of Ms. XXXX. They submit the following: * Ms. XXXX did not diligently complete their BOC forms and failed to amend question 1(E) to reflect their ethnicity as Mohajirs; * Ms. XXXX did not advise them of the legal test they had to meet; * Ms. XXXX was not adequately prepared for their hearing as she failed to meet with them earlier than a few days before their hearing; failed to obtain a full account of the facts behind their claims; failed to question the principal Appellant regarding his ethnicity based fear; failed to make submissions regarding the Appellants' ethnicity; and failed to provide adequate research and independent evidence regarding the mistreatment of Mohajirs in Islamabad; * Ms. XXXX failed to prepare and question the principal Appellant regarding the fears of the minor children and did not make submissions accordingly; * Ms. XXXX failed to question the principal Appellant's son, wife and adult daughter (associate Appellants) about their fear of return; * Ms. XXXX conceded that there was no nexus to a Convention ground at the hearing without advising the Appellants; whereas the claim was based on imputed political opinion and membership in a social group; * Ms. XXXX failed to make meaningful submissions and did not refer to supporting personal documents; * Ms. XXXX failed to refer to the Chairperson's guidelines on Child refugee claimants; * Ms. XXXX told the Appellants that their hearing was perfect; and * Ms. XXXX told the Appellants after they asked why they had received a negative decision that she and the RPD member did not like each other.

The RAD has considered the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) practice notice regarding allegations against former counsel and finds that the appropriate steps were not taken by the Appellants regarding their allegations against Ms. XXXX. It is stated in the notice that: 5. Where the person alleges that they have been inadequately represented by their former counsel, the person must first provide former counsel with: a. a written statement containing the allegations, or in the case of an appeal to the RAD, a copy of the Appellant's Memorandum or other document in the RAD proceedings that contain the allegations; b. a written notice that former counsel has ten days after receiving the allegations to provide a written response to the person, to the applicable Division, and to the Minister (if the Minister is a party to the proceeding); c. a signed authorization releasing any privilege, including solicitor-client privilege, to the extent necessary to allow former counsel to respond to the allegations; and d. a copy of this Practice Notice or information describing where this Practice Notice can be found on the IRB website 6. The person must then provide to the Division a copy of documents (a) to (c) above, as well as proof that the documents (a) to (d) above have been provided to the person's former counsel. 7. Former counsel who intends to respond to the allegations must provide a written response to the person, to the Division, and to the Minister (if the Minister is a party to the proceeding), no later than ten days after receiving the allegations. 8. The person may provide a written reply to the Division, accompanied by proof that this reply was first provided to former counsel and to the Minister (if the Minister is a party to the proceeding). The written reply must be provided no later than five days after the person received former counsel's response.

The RAD notes that there is no evidence in the record that the Appellants complied with items 5, 6, or 8 of the practice notice. It does not appear that former counsel has been notified of the allegations against her or that the Appellants have signed an authorization releasing Ms. XXXX from any privilege, including solicitor client privilege, to allow her to respond to the allegations. The RAD finds therefore that little weight can be put on the allegations against the former counsel regarding her conduct and competence without her having had an opportunity to respond.

However, the RAD has reviewed the record in light of these allegations. The RAD notes that the BOC narrative was eleven pages long and contained detailed information regarding events that occurred in Pakistan and the Appellants' fear of return. All of the adult Appellants signed the BOC declaration stating that all the information contained in the form was complete, true and correct. All of the Appellants adopted the BOC narrative of the principal Appellant for the purpose of the RPD process. The RAD finds that it is reasonable in the circumstances that the RPD member chose only to question the principal Appellant. There is no evidence in the record that counsel for the Appellants or the Appellants indicated in any way that the associate Appellants wished to provide testimony. The Appellants submitted 340 pages of documentary evidence for the hearing, which included personal documents, letters, and country condition documentation. Given the fulsomeness of the BOC narrative and the extensive supporting documentation, the RAD finds that it was reasonable that the hearing into these claims was not lengthy.

The RAD further notes that although the RPD did not refer to IRB guidelines in its decision, it is the expectation that all relevant guidelines are considered by the RPD member in the panel's analysis of a claim, whether or not counsel for the claimant has provided submissions in regard to the guidelines. Furthermore, it is also the expectation that the RPD will assess a claim under both sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA whether or not specific submissions have been made by counsel for the claimant in that regard. The determinative issue in this claim was IFA. Although the RPD wrote in the decision that the fear of criminality did not lead to a nexus to a Convention ground, it does appear that the claim was ultimately assessed under both sections 96 and 97 as the RPD found that the Appellants would not face a serious possibility of persecution, or on a balance of probabilities a personal risk of harm in Islamabad.

The RAD has further considered that IRB members are guided by a Code of Conduct which states that IRB members shall conduct themselves in a manner that will not cast doubt on their ability to perform their duties objectively. The RAD has reviewed the record and finds that it contains nothing to indicate that there was any animosity between the Appellants' former counsel Ms. XXXX and the RPD member, or that the RPD member conducted herself in any way that would have cast doubt on her ability to perform her job objectively. Additionally, the RAD has considered the Federal Court jurisprudence which states that there is a strong presumption of judicial impartiality that is not easily displaced and accordingly the test for a reasonable apprehension of bias requires a "real likelihood or probability of bias".10 The RAD finds that even if Ms. XXXX and the RPD member did not like each other, there is no evidence in the record that this in any way affected the member's conduct or even counsel's conduct during the hearing. There is no evidence in the record to indicate in any way that the RPD decision was biased because of animosity between the member and counsel, or for any other reason.

For all the reasons mentioned above, the RAD finds that little weight can be given to the Appellants' allegations that their former counsel, Ms. XXXX, was incompetent when representing them during the RPD process. Guidelines on Child Refugee Claimants and Claims of the Minor Appellants

The RPD designated the principal Appellant to represent the two minor associate Appellants who were 16 and 11 years old at the time of the hearing. When assessing the claims of all the family members in the decision, the RPD found that the family would be able to relocate to Islamabad and live in relative peace and security in that city which is considered an ethnically and religiously diverse location.

The Appellants argue that the RPD could not simply treat the children as if they were adults with the capacity to endure prejudice and discrimination. They submit that the RPD should have assessed the documentary evidence relevant to the circumstances of the two Mohajir children and should have considered aspects such as education, employment prospects and vulnerability to discrimination and persecution faced by the Mohajir community.

The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to recognize the minor claimant's rights and failed to recognize what can amount to persecution of a child. They submit that the RPD erred by not considering the threats to abduct and kill the minor Appellants.

The RAD has reviewed the Chairperson's Guideline 3: Child and Refugee Claimants and Evidentiary Issues. In reference to this guideline, the minor children at the time of the hearing would have been considered to be accompanied minors. It is noted in the guideline that the best interests of the child must be considered from a procedural aspect and will depend on the circumstances of each case. It is further noted that a child claimant may be called upon to provide evidence through oral testimony about his or her claim and that the child has a right to be heard. Specific considerations are noted in the guideline should the panel need to hear from the child. The RAD notes that the RPD explicitly stated at the hearing that the panel did not have any questions for other members of the family and asked the Appellants' counsel whether she had any questions for the other Appellants to which she replied that she did not.

The RAD has considered the Appellants' argument that the minor children could be kidnapped and killed. The RAD finds that although the RPD did not refer to that specific fear in the decision, it is clear that the RPD had assessed the documentary evidence regarding the situation in Islamabad, the proposed IFA, and found that all of the Appellants could relocate to that city without a risk of harm from the agents of persecution. The RPD found that it was unlikely that XXXX XXXX would have the willingness or ability to seek the Appellants across the country three years after they last had contact. The RAD has considered that when questioned at the hearing about whether the Appellants had any fears about living in Islamabad other than concerns about the agent of persecution finding them there, the principal Appellant spoke about harassment from the police and stated that he could not risk taking his children there because he had already suffered the kidnapping of his son. The principal Appellant was asked again whether there were any other concerns about the proposed IFA and he referred to police harassment and his fear that he would be implicated in a case for monetary reasons. The RAD notes that he did not testify about any other problems he and members of his family would face should they relocate to Islamabad, despite being asked more than once about his concerns.

The RAD notes that the principal Appellant made no comments or allegations regarding treatment his children would receive because of their ethnic background. The RAD agrees with the RPD, as will be noted below, that both prongs of the IFA test have been met in regard to Islamabad and finds that the RPD conducted an adequate assessment of the viability of the IFA for the whole family based on the Appellants' allegations and the testimony provided by the principal Appellant. Ethnicity and Assessment of Personal Evidence

The RPD was satisfied that the events prompting the Appellants to flee Pakistan had taken place. The RPD found based on the presumption of truthfulness, the principal Appellant's consistent testimony and the corroborative documents, that the Appellants' allegations were credible. However, the RPD found that the Appellants have a viable IFA in Islamabad.

The Appellants argue that the RPD had established that the Appellants are Mohajirs at the hearing and yet failed to establish a nexus based on ethnicity. They submit that the RPD failed to acknowledge that there is systematic discrimination and mistreatment of Mohajirs in Pakistan.

The Appellants submit that the RPD misconstrued evidence that the principal Appellant was mistreated by XXXX XXXX in Lahore which related to their ethnicity and the systematic discrimination and mistreatment of Mohajirs in Pakistan.

The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to analyze all the elements of their claim which included the political opinion imputed on the principal Appellant by the police in Lahore who accused him of being a terrorist and a member of the XXXX.

The Appellants submit that the RPD did not consider the principal Appellant's testimony that he could not live anywhere other than in Karachi because he had a bad experience with XXXX XXXX in Lahore, and would be harassed anywhere in the country in that way; because there is a cultural difference and even neighbours do not trust newcomers in a community; and because XXXX XXXX treat newcomers as suspicious persons.
The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to analyse the political opinion imputed on them by the XXXX, as Mohajir opposed to the XXXX are severely mistreated by that party.

The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to analyse the risk from the agents of persecution in Islamabad, given that the RPD found them to be credible and they had stated that the XXXX had sufficient ties with XXXX XXXX which would allow XXXX XXXX to find them in Islamabad. They submit that the RPD erred by not considering the documentary evidence which establishes that Mohajirs face severe competition from mainly Punjabis, who control government and military throughout Pakistan.
The Appellants submit that the RPD had a duty to consider the sur place claim.

The RAD has reviewed the record and finds that the Appellants did not put forward an argument at the RPD hearing or in their BOCs that they fear of persecution in Pakistan based on their ethnic identity as Mohajirs. The RAD does note that the principal Appellant identified himself as a Mohajir early on at the RPD hearing. Furthermore, he stated at the hearing and in his BOC narrative that when he was living in Lahore he was approached by the police who asked to look at his documents which identified him as being from Karachi, and that he was told by the policeman that he must be an XXXX terrorist on the run. He stated that another time the police came to his home in Lahore and accused him of being an Indian agent. He stated that the police made these accusations both times in order to have him pay a bribe.

The RAD finds that this information was all before the RPD when it conducted its assessment of the viability of Islamabad as an IFA. The RPD addressed this information in its decision and found that the Appellants were speculating as to how the police in Islamabad would behave. The RPD considered their submission that the documentary evidence states that police generally harassed displaced persons in Pakistan and found that the Appellants' putative relocation to Islamabad could be distinguished from the experience of internally displaced persons who relocate because of conditions such as armed conflict and natural disasters. The RPD found that the Appellants were affluent, educated, urban people relocating for personal reasons and that it was unlikely that they would face the same disadvantages, vulnerabilities and police attention as compared to, for example, Pashtuns escaping from Khyber Pakthunkhawa.

The RAD has further considered that the principal Appellant was questioned about his reasons for rejecting Islamabad as a potential IFA in Pakistan. He testified that he feared that the gang would find him in Islamabad; that in the rest of the country police would harass them; that there is a language problem and a cultural difference; that the police and neighbours would consider him a suspicious person; and that he could not risk any of his children being kidnapped. Furthermore, he stated that because there is so much terrorism in Islamabad the police look at every person suspiciously. The principal Appellant did not testify to discrimination and persecution based solely on Mohajir ethnicity.

The RAD finds that the RPD did consider the Appellants' concerns, and found that although there was evidence of police corruption, including demands for bribes, there was insufficient evidence to demonstrate that this corruption was systemic. The RPD found that the documentary evidence suggested that obtaining effective state protection or avoiding arrest for those who would otherwise face arrest was affected by police corruption, but that there was insufficient evidence to suggest that the police randomly or systematically demand bribes from those who have not come to their attention. The RPD noted that despite living in Pakistan for most of their lives, the Appellants were only approached for bribes by the police on two occasions and did not otherwise have problems in that regard. The RPD found that the Appellants had not established that there was a serious risk of persecution or on a balance of probabilities a risk of harm in Islamabad, and that it was reasonable for the Appellants to relocate there considering their personal circumstances and that the city is an ethnically and religiously diverse location.

The RAD has conducted its own assessment of the viability of an IFA in Islamabad and whether the Appellants would be safe there. The RAD agrees with the RPD that the agent of persecution in Karachi, the XXXX XXXX gang, is local to that city. The documentary evidence provided by the Appellants does not indicate that this gang has a base of operations in Islamabad. Although the documentary evidence does state that there are targeted killings and kidnappings in urban Sindh, particularly Karachi, affecting both Mohajirs and Sindhis,11 there is insufficient evidence to suggest that those crimes against Mohajirs extend to other parts of the country. The RAD has considered the information request12 regarding the situation and treatment of Mohajirs in Islamabad and notes that the only concern documented was that they faced severe competition for and discrimination in government jobs.

The RAD has considered that the population of Pakistan is approximately 200 million and that the Mohajir population constitutes 7.5%. The RAD finds that there is insufficient evidence to indicate that this group of approximately 14 million people are systemically targeted for extortion or harm within Pakistan. Although the Appellants have alleged that once it is discovered from their identity documents that they are from Karachi, they will be targeted by the police for extortion, the RAD finds that there is insufficient evidence in the record or in the new documents provided by the Appellants that coming from Karachi would cause them to automatically be targeted anywhere in the country. The RAD notes that the US Department of State Report13 states that in Karachi political parties and their affiliated gangs continue to vie for political and economic control and engage in a turf war over extortion collection privileges. This however does not appear to extend to the rest of the country. It is also noted in this document that there were reports of harassment and extortion of Afghani refugees by provincial authorities, police, and host communities. As noted by the RPD, the Appellants would not fall into this category.

The RAD notes that the Appellants have provided a newspaper article stating that a Peshawar policeman was abducted in Islamabad. It is written in the article that police teams were formed to recover him.14 The RAD finds that this situation can be distinguished from the Appellants' given that this individual was a member of the police force. The Appellants do not have high profiles as government or police employees and there is no indication on the record that they have ever had any political involvement.

The RAD has also considered a newspaper article stating that the XXXX was taking part in upcoming elections in 2018 and that the XXXX would field candidates in Islamabad as well as other cities.15 However there is no indication in the article that the XXXX or associated gangs had established a base in that city. The RAD finds that there is insufficient evidence in the record or in the new documents accepted into evidence on appeal that the XXXX or its associated criminal gang have ties in Islamabad that would allow them to find the Appellant in that city which is at the other end of the country from their base in Karachi.

The RAD has considered that there is evidence that in Karachi much of the ethnic violence in recent years has involved turf wars between rival criminal groups backed by political parties, such as the Awami National Party (ANP), a Pashtun nationalist party, and the MQM, which represents the interests of the Mohajir community.16 However, there is no mention that this sort of turf war exists in Islamabad.

The RAD has further considered the documentary evidence which notes that Islamabad has a population of around two million people, including a large number of internal migrants from all parts of the country. There is a strong security presence, including checkpoints throughout the city and its entry points, and patrols by the paramilitary Rangers. These security measures provide a strong deterrent to militant groups planning attacks in the capital, and large-scale militant or sectarian attacks in Islamabad are rare. Such violence more often takes the form of targeted killings (such as drive-by shootings) of high-profile community leaders.17 The Appellants have not identified as community leaders or being involved in any sort of politics.

It is noted in the documentation that the government continued to use the military to support domestic security in Islamabad. Paramilitary forces, including Rangers and the Frontier Constabulary (FC), provided security to some areas of Islamabad18 .

The RAD finds, as did the RPD, that the Appellants would be able to safely relocate to Islamabad without fear of being targeted by the gang from Karachi or any other source. The RAD further finds that given their personal circumstances, relocating to Islamabad would be reasonable. As noted by the RPD they are educated and the principal Appellant has extensive business experience which would enable him to earn a living for the family. There is no evidence in the record that the Appellants would be unable to find appropriate housing or education should any of them wish to continue their education. The RAD finds that there is insufficient information in the record or in the new documents accepted with the appeal to indicate that the Appellants would experience discrimination in any form amounting to persecution in Islamabad. Although there is evidence that there are difficulties for Mohajirs in government employment, the Appellants have not alleged that they wish to work for the government or have had any experience in that regard.

The RAD finds, after considering all of the evidence, and given the Appellants' past and present circumstances, that Islamabad is a viable IFA for them and that there is not a serious possibility that they would suffer persecution in Islamabad or on a balance of probabilities a personal risk of harm in Islamabad. Gender Guidelines

The Appellants provided an amended memorandum which additionally argued that the RPD failed to consider the IRB's Gender Guidelines.19 They argue that the RPD failed to analyse whether the female Appellants suffered persecution for reasons pertaining to kinship, and that there is new evidence of gender-based violence due to imputed political views and refusal to pay extortion demands by the principal Appellant. The Appellants, however have not specifically cited in their amended memorandum which new evidence they are referring to.

The RAD has reviewed the new evidence submitted by the Appellants and notes that in the letter from the principal Appellant's brother-in-law, he writes to his sister, the associate Appellant, "now that your daughters of grown-up, we fear that, God forbid, in your case you and your family come back and these people do something bad to your daughters or harm them, it will be the death of us." However, the RAD notes that this fear is not supported by any accompanying country condition documents and finds that this fear is speculative in regard to what could happen to the female Appellants. Although it is written in the letter that XXXX XXXX is often seen with a senator belonging to XXXX and keeps visiting Karachi, Islamabad and the entire province of Punjab, this statement is not backed up by country condition documentation. The RAD finds that this letter is not probative in establishing that XXXX XXXX has established himself in Islamabad, given that the letter provides no indication as to the source of the information or how this information was acquired by the author of the letter.

The RAD has considered its finding that Islamabad is a viable IFA for all of the Appellants and finds that the new evidence is not probative in establishing that there is a gender-based fear of persecution in that city based on new evidence provided by the Appellants. The RAD further notes that the Appellants did not identify a gender-based fear of persecution in their BOC or at the hearing. The RAD finds that the RPD did not err by failing to analyse whether the female Appellants suffered persecution for reasons pertaining to kinship and gender-based violence. Summary

The RAD has conducted an independent assessment of the all of the evidence contained in the RPD record as well as the new documents allowed with the appeal. The RAD has considered the Appellants' arguments contained in the memorandum and the amended memorandum. The RAD finds that the Appellants have not established they were denied natural justice because of their former counsel's conduct. The RAD finds that the Appellants have a viable IFA in Islamabad as they can safely and reasonably reside in that city.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
